questions.q: What was the Bradley-Terry model originally developed for, in 1952?
options: Training neural networks with gradient descent
Ranking competitors, such as chess players, from a record of pairwise match outcomes, without observing an absolute skill score directly
Compressing large statistical tables
Measuring reaction time in psychology experiments
questions.explain: Bradley-Terry models the probability that one competitor beats another as a function of the difference in latent strength values, inferred purely from pairwise outcomes.

questions.q: In the formula P(y_w ≻ y_l | x) = σ(r(x, y_w) − r(x, y_l)), what happens as r(x, y_w) grows much larger than r(x, y_l)?
options: The predicted preference probability approaches 0
The predicted preference probability approaches 1
The formula becomes undefined
The sigmoid output oscillates
questions.explain: As the reward difference grows large and positive, the logistic sigmoid approaches 1, meaning the model predicts the chosen response is very likely to be preferred.

questions.q: What does the Bradley-Terry-derived training loss L(θ) = −E[log σ(r_θ(x,y_w) − r_θ(x,y_l))] push the reward model's parameters to do?
options: Assign identical scores to all responses
Assign a higher score to the chosen response than the rejected response, consistently across the preference dataset
Minimize the absolute value of every reward
Maximize the reward assigned to rejected responses
questions.explain: This is a maximum-likelihood loss derived from the Bradley-Terry formula: minimizing it makes the observed human preferences (chosen over rejected) as likely as possible under the reward model.

questions.q: Why does the Bradley-Terry formula depend only on the difference r(x,y_w) − r(x,y_l), rather than the absolute scale of the rewards?
options: Because absolute scale is computationally expensive to compute
Because human preference judgments only reveal which response is better, not what the zero point or units of "reward" should be — only the difference is meaningful
Because the sigmoid function cannot accept large numbers
Because reward models cannot output negative values
questions.explain: Preference comparisons are inherently about relative ranking, not absolute magnitude, so a formula depending only on the difference matches exactly what the data can tell you.

questions.q: What mathematical property of the logistic sigmoid makes it practical for this training objective?
options: It is discontinuous at zero, forcing hard decisions
It maps any real-valued reward difference to a probability between 0 and 1 and is smooth and differentiable everywhere, so gradient-based training works cleanly
It only accepts non-negative inputs
It converts rewards into a Discrete action space
questions.explain: The sigmoid's smoothness and (0,1) range make it ideal for turning an unbounded reward difference into a well-behaved, differentiable preference probability usable in a gradient-descent loss.
